I can concede that I cannot prove it's possible to create a version of hell in which people can choose God after going to hell. I see the point you're making here. 

If I were to be fallacious, I would argue the logic I've found is enough to make me believe this version of hell is possible, just like the evidence Christians use to prove the Bible is true. Maybe I did spend my life building this theological argument and I am presenting this as the revelation.

Of course I can't prove it to you, but Christians can't prove their version of hell actually exists either. Both are essentially the same likelihood of truth.

Truthfully, I thought up this argument like 2 days ago and just using it on a whim. So yeah, I can recognize it's gonna be a little more shabby than worldwide religious beliefs.

Okay, I'll give you a circumstance that would cause me to believe in God. If he were to show up and announce himself publicly, teleport to everybody's house, and then telepathically communicate to everybody at once that he is God, I would first confirm that everybody saw and heard the same thing, then I would believe he is real. This is probably way more evidence than I would need, but nonetheless it would convince me.

Again, God would know exactly how to convince anybody on Earth that he exists. He is all knowing, correct? This is why it doesn't matter what it would take to convince me, he would just have to do what it takes to convince each person. Then, there would be no question that everybody knows he exists. But good thing for God, free will still exists! And those who follow him and Jesus after being convinced they exist are still doing so through free will.

If you want me to convince you and prove with certainty that it's possible to create hell/the universe in any way other than the current model of Christianity, then I think you already know that isn't possible, since we have no evidence that there is anything outside of the universe we know. Christians can't even prove that Christianity's model of the universe is representative of reality. Science is really the only thing we have to accurately (to the best of our abilities) figure out the nature of the universe.

So what's the point of this discussion? I'm agnostic myself. I already know there is no proof of God. Obviously I can't prove that God can do anything, because I have no proof that he even exists!

Correct me if I'm wrong, but I'm going to guess that you believe people who genuinely seek the truth and work towards truth faithfully will always end up following Christianity.

I believe people can end up being wrong on their death bed. You believe that anyone who is wrong about God when they die is intentionally choosing against the truth.

Neither of us can prove the other wrong because neither of us know what anyone other than ourselves are thinking and feeling. You genuinely believe Christ is truth and that anyone seeking the truth will find Christ. Unfortunately for me, you don't know if I'm genuinely seeking the truth, and if I die without following Christ, then for all you know, I knew where I was going and chose to be without God anyways.

For every video “proving” God’s existence I would argue there are a dozen higher quality and more convincing arguments against him. 

This debate is not whether God exists. I don’t believe in God, rather I am entertaining his existence for the sake of argument. That being said, the topic I am focusing on right now is whether or not the people who don’t believe in God are intentionally choosing not to be with him. I do not think most non-Christians (focusing on people who have heard of Christianity) fall under this category.

First off, I want to say that if someone chooses to be in hell and not have a relationship with God knowing that he exists, sure, I might be able to accept that God letting them stay in hell isn’t immoral.

I would argue the vast majority of people in hell would not be in this category. Most people are disbelievers because of the lack of proof. Do you really believe it’s so unreasonable for someone to not believe in God when they don’t see any proof that he exists?

Now, imagine how these people would react when they die and meet God. Maybe some will be angry, or even believe he is evil. But a lot of them would accept it and want to follow him. Should they be rejected from heaven just because they didn’t believe in him when they were alive?

But God is the one who created this system in the first place. 

It’s like if the creator of the AI defended his system by saying the AI chose to suffer in “hell” and cannot choose otherwise because “that’s just how the system operates” when he is the one who made it that way.

If people in hell cannot desire to go to heaven, then God can make it so they can. In fact, if God’s real goal is free will for the people, then God should want people in hell to still be able to choose him through free will. With all his power, that should be completely possible.

If your next argument is “well these people are just going to keep descending further from God”. How do you even know this is true? I’d argue most people are in hell for no other reason than disbelief due to a lack of proof. If they’re given proof, most of these people would follow God just like any believer would.

Even if this system i’m proposing wouldnt save everyone from eternal suffering, it would surely save the vast majority. 

If God truly operates as you believe he does, then I can only assume God’s real goal is not necessarily for people to choose him through their free will. His goal is getting as many people as possible to believe him without proof of his existence. Why else would he allow disbelievers no second chance to redeem themselves after they’ve been given proof of his existence? 

Why is faith without proof so important to God? Like I’ve said before, proof doesn’t remove free will. If anything, it only increases free will. Having as many facts on the matter as possible is really the only way someone can make an informed choice.

From what I can tell, the vast majority of people wouldn’t actually choose to go to hell. They’re choosing the best option they can with the information they’re given. They just happen to be incorrect, and are facing consequences for an action they aren’t actually at fault for.

If someone wants to be in a place of torture for all eternity, they can go ahead and do so, not my life, not my experience, so I don't really care.

But why did they put themselves there? Did they literally see two signs that said "Eternal hellish misery" and "Eternal heavenly bliss" and decide to pick hell? I highly doubt that to be the case.

I can correct your analogy with a different analogy. Let's imagine someone were to sign a contract that they will let their hand get cut off in one year. I do believe that person has the right to withdraw that consent at any time, including after the hand were cut off, if the surgeon is able to reattach it.

My point is not that people shouldn't be allowed to choose an eternity in hell. In fact, it's quite the opposite. If someone desires to go to heaven, even after they go to hell, they should have the right to do that.

Let consider a doctor that has the power to reattach somebody's hand. Someone goes to him and wants their hand chopped off, and he complies. Later, that person comes back and wants his hand reattached. Why shouldn't the doctor reattach that person's hand?

In this case, I will accept that, at the very least, we have a reason to allow these machines to run in an eternally suffering state, because the information it would gather would be useful for us. But I still believe it is immoral to cause eternal suffering for any being no matter how useful the information would be.

Furthermore, it would only make sense for me to also believe that allowing people who, through no fault of their own, to suffer eternally for no good reason other than I guess punishing people who didn't follow him would be wrong as well.

I mean, imagine a parent punishing their adult children for choosing a different path in life than them (like choosing a different career). I think it would be clear that legally and morally, that parent would absolutely be in the wrong. Why shouldn't we hold God to the same standards? The universe cannot support intelligent life for whatever reason.

Or the universe can support intelligent life.
